# Stonebeck: the gate as confession, not circuit-breaker

Rating: underweight

Calder & Root read the redemption gate as friction that policy support will dissolve.¹ We read it as the mechanism by which a marked book finally admits what secondary prices have been saying for weeks. Bids quoted in the low 80s are not a liquidity event; they are a valuation event that the official marks have not yet caught up to — hence a reported_vs_public_gap of +1.0%, small in isolation but directionally consistent with a book that lags its own collateral.

The headline numbers invite complacency. one_year_return of +6.0% and ytd_return of -3.5% can be read as a pause in an otherwise sound compounding story. We would note instead that the ytd figure is the more recent, more informative print, and that it arrived alongside hy_spread_now_bps of 640bps — wide enough to signal genuine credit stress, not mere seasonal noise. Layer on policy_rate_now at 5.25% against cpi_now of 3.8%: real rates remain restrictive by any conventional measure, which is precisely the condition under which gated vehicles discover their fragilities rather than resolve them.

Picture the chart: drawdown at -3.0% sits as a shallow trough on the page, almost reassuring next to the taller bar of hy_spread_now_bps — the spread bar dwarfs the drawdown bar by an order of magnitude, and it is the spread, not the drawdown, that should be setting the scale of concern here.²

The explicit risk to this view: gates can also reflect prudent liability management rather than insolvency, and if policy eases faster than the curve implies, spreads could compress before marks are forced to adjust — leaving underweight positioning early.

---
¹ "Stay the course" presumes the course was accurately charted.
² A trough that shallow, next to a spread that wide, is not a coincidence we're prepared to ignore.
